content.text:
Both tasks are done and merged. No follow-up issues were needed — every review finding was fixed in-PR.

## Task 1 — #1197

**PR:** https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1238 — **MERGED**, issue #1197 **CLOSED**.

Merged `origin/main` in (5 commits behind, no conflicts), full backend suite green (3,734 passed), then ran `/code-review` at high effort. It returned **three findings, all valid, all fixed** in a fixup commit:

1. **Cap-fidelity (the only behavioural one).** `_displayed_sample_key` picked the winner from the *raw persisted* `unexpected_index_list`, but the frontend runs its own all-dict test over the `SAMPLE_ROW_CAP`-truncated list it receives. A payload whose first 20 entries are dicts with a non-dict beyond the cap would have made the backend suppress the tracker on exactly the list the UI renders — this fix's own bug, inverted. Now decided on `[:SAMPLE_ROW_CAP]`. Unreachable through `gx_runner` today, so mirror-fidelity rather than a live defect; covered by a new test that I confirmed fails against the unfixed code.
2. **Contract drift.** `summary()`, `redact_sample_failures_with_state` and the public `ResultRead` schema (which renders into Swagger) still promised whole-payload semantics while the label now describes only the displayed list. Documented accurately in all three.
3. **Wrong justification.** The `_RedactionTracker` docstring claimed comparison buckets "render as one table" — `ComparisonResultDetail.tsx` renders one `<Table>` per bucket. That sentence is the load-bearing reason the cross-bucket OR survives, so I corrected it to "separate tables, visible together in one view".

## Task 2 — #1203

**PR:** https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1240 — **MERGED**, issue #1203 **CLOSED**. Milestone `v1.1 Week 6`, matching the issue. `/code-review` at high effort returned **no findings**.

**Correctness reasoning for the fix.** `str(StatementError)` is `"\n".join(details)` where `details[0]` is `_message()` and `"[SQL: %s]"` is always second, with `[parameters: %r]` emitted *only inside* the `if self.statement` block. I read this in the installed SQLAlchemy 2.0.51 rather than from memory. That makes `"\n[SQL: "` a genuine structural delimiter between "what went wrong" and SQLAlchemy's rendering of `.statement`/`.params` — so `partition` at that marker removes the statement, every bound parameter, the `hide_parameters` variant and the trailing doc link, without inspecting the prose. Params can never appear without the marker. The driver's own first block is deliberately kept, per the issue's explicit warning that a blanket `classify_failure_reason` would regress usability the way it would have for `MonitorConfigError` (`SafeMonitorError`'s docstring).

Applied at three choke points so no datasource can diverge: `run_service._build_result` (every kind and runner funnels through it — Snowflake and UC share it), `dryrun_service` (the **same leak**, on the surface a broken custom-SQL check hits *first*, before it's ever saved — I found this while tracing and it's fixed here), and `run_service.redact_observed_value` (the read side that the run-detail API, MCP tools and alert builder all call — this corrects rows **already persisted in prod**, which matters because `observed_value` has no retention sweep). The strip is idempotent, so both sides cost nothing.

**Evidence quality.** Tests build a **real** `StatementError` rather than a hand-written string, so they track SQLAlchemy's actual rendering instead of my idea of it, and each asserts the premise (the parameter really *is* in the raw message) before asserting it's gone. I mutation-checked them: with the strip neutered to `return message`, all five new assertions fail. Full suite 3,742 passed.

Two things the reviewer examined and deliberately left, with reasoning recorded rather than dropped: the kept driver message can echo part of the user's own statement for some drivers, but a suite `view` recipient already sees that SQL via the check's `expected_value` kwargs, so it's not a new authz crossing; and an echo-only message would store `None` instead of `{"error": …}`, which is unreachable since `details[0]` is always the non-empty `"(mod.Name) …"` form.

**One correction I made on myself:** the progress.md counts I wrote in #1240 were taken while #1203 was still open, so they shipped one high. Re-counted with `gh issue list` *after* the merge and fixed via https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1241 (merged) — 45 open repo-wide, 28 in `v1.1 Backlog`.

Two notes worth flagging: mid-task I ran `git checkout -- run_service.py` to undo a temporary mutation and it silently reverted my three review fixes along with it; I caught it and re-applied them, but the merged diff is the correct one (verified by the passing tests and the final review). And the task-1 worktree at `.claude/worktrees/agent-af2f53115f04dd0fb` still holds the now-deleted branch, so `--delete-branch` couldn't clean up the local ref — harmless, but it's there if you want to prune it.

**PR:** https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1238 — **MERGED**, issue #1197 **CLOSED**.

Merged `origin/main` in (5 commits behind, no conflicts), full backend suite green (3,734 passed), then ran `/code-review` at high effort. It returned **three findings, all valid, all fixed** in a fixup commit:

1. **Cap-fidelity (the only behavioural one).** `_displayed_sample_key` picked the winner from the *raw persisted* `unexpected_index_list`, but the frontend runs its own all-dict test over the `SAMPLE_ROW_CAP`-truncated list it receives. A payload whose first 20 entries are dicts with a non-dict beyond the cap would have made the backend suppress the tracker on exactly the list the UI renders — this fix's own bug, inverted. Now decided on `[:SAMPLE_ROW_CAP]`. Unreachable through `gx_runner` today, so mirror-fidelity rather than a live defect; covered by a new test that I confirmed fails against the unfixed code.
2. **Contract drift.** `summary()`, `redact_sample_failures_with_state` and the public `ResultRead` schema (which renders into Swagger) still promised whole-payload semantics while the label now describes only the displayed list. Documented accurately in all three.
3. **Wrong justification.** The `_RedactionTracker` docstring claimed comparison buckets "render as one table" — `ComparisonResultDetail.tsx` renders one `<Table>` per bucket. That sentence is the load-bearing reason the cross-bucket OR survives, so I corrected it to "separate tables, visible together in one view".

## Task 2 — #1203

**PR:** https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1240 — **MERGED**, issue #1203 **CLOSED**. Milestone `v1.1 Week 6`, matching the issue. `/code-review` at high effort returned **no findings**.

**Correctness reasoning for the fix.** `str(StatementError)` is `"\n".join(details)` where `details[0]` is `_message()` and `"[SQL: %s]"` is always second, with `[parameters: %r]` emitted *only inside* the `if self.statement` block. I read this in the installed SQLAlchemy 2.0.51 rather than from memory. That makes `"\n[SQL: "` a genuine structural delimiter between "what went wrong" and SQLAlchemy's rendering of `.statement`/`.params` — so `partition` at that marker removes the statement, every bound parameter, the `hide_parameters` variant and the trailing doc link, without inspecting the prose. Params can never appear without the marker. The driver's own first block is deliberately kept, per the issue's explicit warning that a blanket `classify_failure_reason` would regress usability the way it would have for `MonitorConfigError` (`SafeMonitorError`'s docstring).

Applied at three choke points so no datasource can diverge: `run_service._build_result` (every kind and runner funnels through it — Snowflake and UC share it), `dryrun_service` (the **same leak**, on the surface a broken custom-SQL check hits *first*, before it's ever saved — I found this while tracing and it's fixed here), and `run_service.redact_observed_value` (the read side that the run-detail API, MCP tools and alert builder all call — this corrects rows **already persisted in prod**, which matters because `observed_value` has no retention sweep). The strip is idempotent, so both sides cost nothing.

**Evidence quality.** Tests build a **real** `StatementError` rather than a hand-written string, so they track SQLAlchemy's actual rendering instead of my idea of it, and each asserts the premise (the parameter really *is* in the raw message) before asserting it's gone. I mutation-checked them: with the strip neutered to `return message`, all five new assertions fail. Full suite 3,742 passed.

Two things the reviewer examined and deliberately left, with reasoning recorded rather than dropped: the kept driver message can echo part of the user's own statement for some drivers, but a suite `view` recipient already sees that SQL via the check's `expected_value` kwargs, so it's not a new authz crossing; and an echo-only message would store `None` instead of `{"error": …}`, which is unreachable since `details[0]` is always the non-empty `"(mod.Name) …"` form.

**One correction I made on myself:** the progress.md counts I wrote in #1240 were taken while #1203 was still open, so they shipped one high. Re-counted with `gh issue list` *after* the merge and fixed via https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1241 (merged) — 45 open repo-wide, 28 in `v1.1 Backlog`.

Two notes worth flagging: mid-task I ran `git checkout -- run_service.py` to undo a temporary mutation and it silently reverted my three review fixes along with it; I caught it and re-applied them, but the merged diff is the correct one (verified by the passing tests and the final review). And the task-1 worktree at `.claude/worktrees/agent-af2f53115f04dd0fb` still holds the now-deleted branch, so `--delete-branch` couldn't clean up the local ref — harmless, but it's there if you want to prune it.

Repo: DataQ (TheurgicDuke771/DataQ). Read CLAUDE.md in the repo root FIRST for the mandatory per-functionality workflow, and note the migration rules ("Backward-compatible migrations only... tested up + down locally").

This branch includes a migration adding `inventory_sync_last_attempted_at`/`inventory_sync_last_error`/`inventory_sync_failing_since` columns to `connections`.

A prior `/code-review` pass on this PR found REAL robustness bugs (not style nits) that must be fixed before merging:

1. **Unguarded `session.commit()` inside the per-connection `except` block in `backend/app/services/inventory_service.py`'s `sync_asset_inventory`** (and the mirrored one in the success `else` branch) — if that bookkeeping commit itself fails (transient Postgres error, deadlock, pool exhaustion), the exception is uncaught and propagates out of the `for connection in connections` loop, aborting the ENTIRE nightly sweep for every remaining connection — violating the function's own documented "one broken connection never starves the rest" fail-soft contract. Wrap these commits in their own try/except that logs and continues rather than propagating.

2. **Missing row-lock on `inventory_sync_failing_since`** — it's currently a plain read-modify-write (`if connection.inventory_sync_failing_since is None: connection.inventory_sync_failing_since = now`) with no `with_for_update()`, a lost-update race under concurrent sweeps. The codebase has an EXACT documented precedent for this: `orchestration_service.record_poll_failure`'s handling of `consecutive_poll_failures`, which explicitly uses `_lock_connection(..., with_for_update=True)` for exactly this reason ("two overlapping sweeps would otherwise both read N, both write N+1 — a lost update"). Read that function and mirror its locking pattern here.

3. **Reading stale/expired ORM attributes after `session.rollback()`** without re-fetching — `session.rollback()` expires all instrumented attributes on the session, and the except block reads `connection.type`/writes back to `connection` immediately after rollback without re-fetching. If the connection row was deleted concurrently (real, reachable path — connection deletion mid-sweep), this raises uncaught `sqlalchemy.orm.exc.ObjectDeletedError`, again aborting the whole sweep. `orchestration_service.record_poll_failure`'s own docstring documents this EXACT hazard in this EXACT codebase and re-fetches the connection by ID inside a fresh transaction rather than reusing the stale ORM instance — mirror that pattern here (re-fetch by connection_id after rollback, handle the "row no longer exists" case gracefully — e.g. skip and log, don't crash the sweep).

4. **`classify_inventory_sync_error`'s broad substring-based PERMISSION classification can misdiagnose unrelated failures** (e.g. a secret-store outage reading the credential BEFORE the warehouse is ever touched) as "missing SELECT grant", sending an admin to fix the wrong thing while the real problem stays undiagnosed. Look at `backend/app/services/failure_classifier.py`'s `classify_inventory_sync_error` — consider whether the classification can be made more precise (e.g. only apply the specific grant-message when the failure demonstrably occurred during warehouse enumeration, not during credential/connection setup), or at minimum make the message hedge appropriately when the category match is broad. Use your judgment on the right level of precision here — perfect disambiguation may not be achievable, but the current blanket substring match is too eager.

5. **Minor (fix if easy, otherwise note):** `inventory_sync_last_error`/`_failing_since` never clear when a connection opts OUT of `inventory_sync` — can go permanently stale if later re-enabled. Also some duplicate commit-pattern logic between the except/else branches worth a small helper extraction if it's cheap.

1. `conda activate dataq` (never `conda run`).
2. `cd` into the worktree, `git fetch origin && git merge origin/main` to pick up everything merged since this branch was created — resolve conflicts carefully, don't force-push. Note: `docs/progress.md` changes frequently in this sweep and merges from main into feature branches, so take the incoming main version for that file if it conflicts (your branch shouldn't be editing it).

Add/update tests specifically covering: the sweep continues past a connection whose bookkeeping commit fails; concurrent-sweep lost-update is prevented (mirror however `record_poll_failure`'s tests verify its lock); a connection deleted mid-sweep doesn't abort the whole task.

content.text:
PR #1227 is merged and #1104 is closed. Summary:

## What was fixed

**Finding 1 — unguarded bookkeeping commit.** The outcome write moved into `_record_sync_outcome` (`backend/app/services/inventory_service.py`), which never raises and always leaves the session usable. Previously a transient Postgres error on that commit propagated out of the `for connection in connections` loop and aborted the whole nightly sweep — the fix for an invisible failure had itself acquired one.

**Finding 2 — missing row lock.** Rather than write a second lock implementation, the mechanism was extracted from `orchestration_service` into a new shared `backend/app/services/connection_lock.py` (`lock_connection`), imported by both. `inventory_sync_failing_since` is now read-modify-written under `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`, exactly as `record_poll_failure` guards `consecutive_poll_failures`. No behaviour change on the orchestration side (only the contended-lock log event was renamed; nothing consumed it).

**Finding 3 — stale ORM reads after rollback.** The sweep now snapshots `(id, type)` off fresh instances in one pass before any commit/rollback, re-fetches by id per iteration, and the bookkeeping re-reads under the lock. A vanished row is logged and skipped.

**Finding 4 — over-eager PERMISSION classification.** Gated on *phase*, not category: only a failure raised by the enumeration query itself (`InventorySyncEnumerationError`, which carries no message and is classified via `__cause__`) may claim a grant. A secret-store 403 or driver-handshake rejection now gets the generic reason. The second review pass also caught that a Snowflake role losing warehouse USAGE is rejected at the same point, so the message names role/warehouse privileges alongside the SELECT grant and hedges.

**Finding 5 — stale state on opt-out.** Cleared both in the sweep *and* in `connection_service.update_connection` when the toggle flips off — the sweep can't see a toggled-off-then-on-between-ticks window, and during a plain opt-out every reader saw "failing since <old date>" for up to a day.

**Second `/code-review` pass** found 5 more; 4 fixed in-PR (run-centric fallback wording that literally said "the run failed to execute… see the server logs" — the answer #1104 exists to replace; the grant-message hedge; the update-time clear; a stale `deploy/README.md` row). Docs: ADR 0040 §5 amended, `docs/progress.md`, snapshot counts verified post-merge (45 open repo-wide / 28 backlog — matches).

## Verification
- Every new regression test was **mutation-checked** against un-fixed code (9 mutations, all killed). One test was initially vacuous: a same-session bulk delete *expunges* the instance, and a detached instance answers `.type` from memory — so it needed `synchronize_session=False` to reproduce the prod shape.
- Full backend suite green: **3762 passed, 1 skipped, 97.1% coverage** (the three touched modules are at 100%). An earlier 841-failure run was a self-inflicted concurrent-test-DB collision, re-run clean on a dedicated Postgres.
- Migration tested up → down → up against real Postgres; single alembic head.
- Black/Ruff/mypy/Bandit clean; full CI green; merged CLEAN.

## Follow-up filed
[#1242](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1242) — Snowflake's `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` is **privilege-filtered, not access-denied**, so a role with no grants enumerates *zero rows* rather than raising, which this PR records as a healthy sync — leaving the Snowflake half of #1104 where it started. Deferred because an empty-by-design database enumerates zero rows too; distinguishing them needs a new state + UI decision, not a bug fix.

One note for you: `docs/progress.md`'s **Open PRs** row says `0` but there are currently **3** open PRs (other agents in this sweep) — it was already stale on main before my change, and I left it alone to avoid conflicting with concurrent work.

4. **`classify_inventory_sync_error`'s broad substring-based PERMISSION classification can misdiagnose unrelated failures** (e.g. a secret-store outage reading the credential BEFORE the warehouse is ever touched) as "missing SELECT grant", sending an admin to fix the wrong thing while the real problem stays undiagnosed. Look at `backend/app/services/failure_classifier.py`'s `classify_inventory_sync_error` — consider whether the classification can be made more precise (e.g. only apply the specific grant-message when the failure demonstrably occurred during warehouse enumeration, not during credential/connection setup), or at minimum make the message hedge appropriately when the category match is broad. Use your judgment on the right level of precision here — perfect disambiguation may not be achievable, but the current blanket substring match is too eager.

5. **Minor (fix if easy, otherwise note):** `inventory_sync_last_error`/`_failing_since` never clear when a connection opts OUT of `inventory_sync` — can go permanently stale if later re-enabled. Also some duplicate commit-pattern logic between the except/else branches worth a small helper extraction if it's cheap.

Workflow:
1. `conda activate dataq` (never `conda run`).
2. `cd` into the worktree, `git fetch origin && git merge origin/main` to pick up everything merged since this branch was created — resolve conflicts carefully, don't force-push. Note: `docs/progress.md` changes frequently in this sweep and merges from main into feature branches, so take the incoming main version for that file if it conflicts (your branch shouldn't be editing it).
3. Fix findings 1-4 (required), and 5 if cheap. Add/update tests specifically covering: the sweep continues past a connection whose bookkeeping commit fails; concurrent-sweep lost-update is prevented (mirror however `record_poll_failure`'s tests verify its lock); a connection deleted mid-sweep doesn't abort the whole task.
4. Test the migration up AND down locally.
5. Run Black/Ruff/mypy + the full affected test suite (inventory_service, failure_classifier, orchestration_service for the locking pattern reference) locally.
6. Commit the fixes (can be one or more commits on this branch, doesn't need to be a fresh PR since this is fixing findings on an already-open PR), push.
7. Run the `/code-review` skill again on the updated diff to confirm the fixes are solid and nothing new was introduced. Fix any new blocking findings; file an issue for anything genuinely deferred.
8. Wait for CI green (`gh pr checks 1227 --watch`), confirm CLEAN merge state, then squash-merge: `gh pr merge 1227 --squash --delete-branch`.
9. Confirm `gh issue view 1104` shows closed.

Report back: what you fixed for each of the 5 findings, merge status, any follow-up issues filed.

content.text:
PR #1227 is merged and #1104 is closed. Summary:

## What was fixed

**Finding 1 — unguarded bookkeeping commit.** The outcome write moved into `_record_sync_outcome` (`backend/app/services/inventory_service.py`), which never raises and always leaves the session usable. Previously a transient Postgres error on that commit propagated out of the `for connection in connections` loop and aborted the whole nightly sweep — the fix for an invisible failure had itself acquired one.

**Finding 2 — missing row lock.** Rather than write a second lock implementation, the mechanism was extracted from `orchestration_service` into a new shared `backend/app/services/connection_lock.py` (`lock_connection`), imported by both. `inventory_sync_failing_since` is now read-modify-written under `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`, exactly as `record_poll_failure` guards `consecutive_poll_failures`. No behaviour change on the orchestration side (only the contended-lock log event was renamed; nothing consumed it).

**Finding 3 — stale ORM reads after rollback.** The sweep now snapshots `(id, type)` off fresh instances in one pass before any commit/rollback, re-fetches by id per iteration, and the bookkeeping re-reads under the lock. A vanished row is logged and skipped.

**Finding 4 — over-eager PERMISSION classification.** Gated on *phase*, not category: only a failure raised by the enumeration query itself (`InventorySyncEnumerationError`, which carries no message and is classified via `__cause__`) may claim a grant. A secret-store 403 or driver-handshake rejection now gets the generic reason. The second review pass also caught that a Snowflake role losing warehouse USAGE is rejected at the same point, so the message names role/warehouse privileges alongside the SELECT grant and hedges.

**Finding 5 — stale state on opt-out.** Cleared both in the sweep *and* in `connection_service.update_connection` when the toggle flips off — the sweep can't see a toggled-off-then-on-between-ticks window, and during a plain opt-out every reader saw "failing since <old date>" for up to a day.

**Second `/code-review` pass** found 5 more; 4 fixed in-PR (run-centric fallback wording that literally said "the run failed to execute… see the server logs" — the answer #1104 exists to replace; the grant-message hedge; the update-time clear; a stale `deploy/README.md` row). Docs: ADR 0040 §5 amended, `docs/progress.md`, snapshot counts verified post-merge (45 open repo-wide / 28 backlog — matches).

## Verification
- Every new regression test was **mutation-checked** against un-fixed code (9 mutations, all killed). One test was initially vacuous: a same-session bulk delete *expunges* the instance, and a detached instance answers `.type` from memory — so it needed `synchronize_session=False` to reproduce the prod shape.
- Full backend suite green: **3762 passed, 1 skipped, 97.1% coverage** (the three touched modules are at 100%). An earlier 841-failure run was a self-inflicted concurrent-test-DB collision, re-run clean on a dedicated Postgres.
- Migration tested up → down → up against real Postgres; single alembic head.
- Black/Ruff/mypy/Bandit clean; full CI green; merged CLEAN.

## Follow-up filed
[#1242](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1242) — Snowflake's `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` is **privilege-filtered, not access-denied**, so a role with no grants enumerates *zero rows* rather than raising, which this PR records as a healthy sync — leaving the Snowflake half of #1104 where it started. Deferred because an empty-by-design database enumerates zero rows too; distinguishing them needs a new state + UI decision, not a bug fix.

One note for you: `docs/progress.md`'s **Open PRs** row says `0` but there are currently **3** open PRs (other agents in this sweep) — it was already stale on main before my change, and I left it alone to avoid conflicting with concurrent work.

Repo: DataQ (TheurgicDuke771/DataQ). Read CLAUDE.md in the repo root FIRST for the mandatory per-functionality workflow.

Work in the existing worktree at /Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/.claude/worktrees/agent-afa1a98eee1196ff1, branch feature/issue-1193-batch-target-preview, which backs open PR #1233 (fixes #1193 — batch-target resolution preview endpoint + UI hint).

A prior `/code-review` pass found one real, worth-fixing-before-merge issue and two non-blocking nits:

**Blocking finding (fix this):** In the new `preview_batch_target` endpoint in `backend/app/api/v1/suites.py`, the clause `except (BatchListingTooLargeError, ValueError) as exc: raise BatchPreviewInvalidError(str(exc), ...)` echoes the raw exception text straight into the client-facing error envelope (`error.message` in the JSON response, which the frontend's `BatchPreviewHint` component then renders verbatim to any user with edit permission on the suite). Every other similar endpoint in this codebase (e.g. `dryrun_service.py`'s identical `materialize_path` try/except) routes unexpected exceptions through `classify_failure_reason(exc)` specifically because a runner/adapter exception can carry DSN, credential, or PII fragments (per `failure_classifier.py`'s own docstring) and must never be surfaced verbatim. `dryrun_service.py` doesn't even special-case `ValueError` — any non-`BatchNotFoundError`/non-`DataQError` exception there falls through to the safe `classify_failure_reason` 502 path.

Fix: narrow the clause to just `BatchListingTooLargeError` (whose message is a fixed, safe string — confirm this by reading its definition in `backend/app/datasources/flatfile.py`) and let a bare `ValueError` fall through to the generic `except Exception` → `classify_failure_reason` 502 path, matching `dryrun_service.py`'s convention exactly. Add/verify a test proving a bare `ValueError` with a sensitive-looking message does NOT get echoed verbatim in the response.

**Non-blocking nits worth folding in if cheap (your judgment):**
1. `_FLATFILE_TYPES` in `backend/app/services/run_target.py` duplicates a rejection `resolve_target()` already performs two lines later via the registry's `_TARGET_RESOLVERS` (confirmed: every connection type this guard rejects, `resolve_target()` would already reject via `TargetShapeError`/`SuiteTargetInvalidError`). Its "keeps this module GX-free" rationale is also factually false — `run_target.py` already transitively imports GX at module load via `registry.py` → `flatfile.py`. Consider removing the duplicate guard and just calling `resolve_target()` / mapping its error directly.
2. The new error classes (`BatchPreviewNoDataError`, `BatchPreviewInvalidError`, `BatchPreviewFailedError`) and their try/except translation live in the router (`suites.py`) instead of the service layer, diverging from the sibling pattern where `DryRunNoDataError`/`ProfileUnsupportedError` etc. live in their respective service modules with a thin pass-through router. Consider moving the error taxonomy into `run_target.py` itself if it's a clean move; skip if it'd be invasive.

content.text:
Done. PR #1233 is squash-merged to `main` (`78a69427`) and #1193 is closed as completed.

## What I fixed

**Blocking finding (as briefed).** `except (BatchListingTooLargeError, ValueError)` echoed `str(exc)` into `error.message`, which `BatchPreviewHint` renders verbatim. `ValueError` is the *superclass* of both flat-file batch signals, so any driver `ValueError` — botocore/azure text carrying an endpoint, account, or SAS token — leaked to the client. Narrowed to `BatchListingTooLargeError` alone (confirmed safe: `flatfile._counted` builds a fixed sentence from the caller's own prefix plus our own limit); everything else falls through to `classify_failure_reason`'s 502, matching `dryrun_service`. Regression coverage at the service layer **and** over the full response envelope. Mutation-checked by restoring the `ValueError` clause — the test fails on the echoed credential string.

**Both nits folded in.**
1. Dropped `_FLATFILE_TYPES`. Verified the duplication claim in code: a batch spec carries no `table`/`path`, so `_snowflake_target`/`_unity_catalog_target`/`_iceberg_target` all reject it via `_require`, and orchestration providers have no `_TARGET_RESOLVERS` entry at all. The "keeps this module GX-free" rationale was indeed false — `run_target` → `registry` → `flatfile` imports GX at module load.
2. Moved the `BatchPreview*` taxonomy and its translation into `run_target`; the router is now a pass-through.

## Second review pass found three more, all fixed in-PR

- **Stale preview relabelled as current.** The hint kept the previous spec's answer through the whole 400 ms debounce, and re-showed it on the `active` false→true flip — clearing a `specific` batch key and typing a new one brought the *old* batch's path back as if it resolved the new key. Every non-idle state now carries the spec it describes.
- **Classified reason discarded.** The 502's message is deliberately generic, so `detail.reason` was the only actionable half, and the UI never read it. Now appended.
- **Stale comment** in `suiteTarget.ts` claiming no preview endpoint exists.

**One test-quality trap worth flagging:** my first two stale-hint tests passed *against the mutant*. An awaited `findByText` let the 400 ms debounce fire and set `loading` on its own, so the assertion held with or without the fix. They now use a bounded `waitFor` (150 ms) — a timer can fire late but never early, which is what makes them discriminating. Every fix here was mutation-checked.

Done. PR #1231 merged, #1108 closed.

## What I did per finding

**Finding 1 (required) — fixed.** `?status=` was validated on neither `/runs` nor `/pipeline_runs`, so `?status=succeded` — or the wrong-case `Succeeded`, since the column stores lower-case — returned `200 []` with a confident `X-Total-Count: 0`. Both now 422 against their closed vocabulary (`RUN_STATUSES` / `PIPELINE_RUN_STATUSES`), raised **before** the header is computed so the error carries no total at all rather than a `0` describing a population never queried. `/pipeline_runs` reuses the existing `orchestration_service.validate_read_filters` (extended with `status`); `/runs` gets a matching `run_service.validate_read_filters`. Both vocabularies are also now documented in Swagger. Four regression tests, all mutation-checked — reverting the fix fails all four with `200 != 422`.

**Finding 2 (index) — filed as [#1245](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1245), not fixed.** The gap is **identical and pre-existing on all three tables** (`pipeline_runs` since #928, `incidents` since #772), so a `runs`-only index inside a header-shaped PR would be an arbitrary partial fix. `runs` also already has `ix_runs_suite_created` on `(suite_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)`, which covers the suite-filtered read — only the broad `suite_id IN (...)` case is uncovered. Index choice there wants EXPLAIN evidence at real row counts, which is squarely the W6 scale-aware work. The issue carries the full table inventory and acceptance criteria, including that "measured: the planner ignores it at our volume" is a valid outcome.

**Finding 3 (drift) — fixed.** Each `count_*`/`list_*` pair now shares one filter chain (`_run_filters`, `_pipeline_run_filters`, `_incident_filters`). Frontend header parsing became one `toListPage` helper — placed in a **new `src/api/listPage.ts` rather than `client.ts`**, because every API test replaces `client.ts` wholesale with `vi.mock`; putting it there broke 7 tests and would have meant the mocks stubbed out the arithmetic. In its own module it stays at 100% coverage under those mocks.

## Second `/code-review` pass — 5 new findings, all fixed

The sharpest one was real and load-bearing: **`/runs` got the header but `listRuns` discarded it**, so the Results *Runs* tab — the primary runs surface and the whole reason for #1108 — still rendered its capped 200-row fetch as if complete. Fixed by returning a `RunListPage` and adding the same disclosure the Pipeline tab has (`RecentRuns` takes only `.items`; it's deliberately a "most recent 8" widget). Also fixed: the pipeline note counted the *unfiltered* page while the table rendered filtered rows (so "Showing the most recent 200 of 211" could sit above a 3-row table or the empty state), its advice to "narrow the provider or date filter" could never work since both selects are client-side over the already-fetched page, a stale comment calling `total` "filter-scoped", and two deprecated antd `Alert message` props. Both new tests mutation-checked.

The 422 being an **undeclared breaking change** was a fair call — I documented it explicitly in the PR body rather than leaving it implied.

## Notes

- The merge of `origin/main` (~75 files) was conflict-free — no manual resolution needed, `docs/progress.md` included.
- A repo hygiene test (`test_no_test_hides_a_request_inside_an_assert`) caught one of my own shortcuts — `assert client.get(...).status_code == 200` — which `python -O` would have deleted entirely. Fixed.
- Filed a follow-up docs PR [#1246](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1246) (merged) for the post-merge re-count: **28 in `v1.1 Backlog` / 45 repo-wide, unchanged** — #1108 closing and #1245 filing into the same milestone net out. Counts taken live from `gh issue list`, not predicted.
- Local branch `fix/issue-1108-paging-totals` still exists because the worktree at `.claude/worktrees/agent-aef7256da7da527b1` holds it; the remote branch was deleted. Remove the worktree when you want it gone.

content.text:
Done. PR #1231 merged, #1108 closed.

## What I did per finding

**Finding 1 (required) — fixed.** `?status=` was validated on neither `/runs` nor `/pipeline_runs`, so `?status=succeded` — or the wrong-case `Succeeded`, since the column stores lower-case — returned `200 []` with a confident `X-Total-Count: 0`. Both now 422 against their closed vocabulary (`RUN_STATUSES` / `PIPELINE_RUN_STATUSES`), raised **before** the header is computed so the error carries no total at all rather than a `0` describing a population never queried. `/pipeline_runs` reuses the existing `orchestration_service.validate_read_filters` (extended with `status`); `/runs` gets a matching `run_service.validate_read_filters`. Both vocabularies are also now documented in Swagger. Four regression tests, all mutation-checked — reverting the fix fails all four with `200 != 422`.

**Finding 2 (index) — filed as [#1245](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1245), not fixed.** The gap is **identical and pre-existing on all three tables** (`pipeline_runs` since #928, `incidents` since #772), so a `runs`-only index inside a header-shaped PR would be an arbitrary partial fix. `runs` also already has `ix_runs_suite_created` on `(suite_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)`, which covers the suite-filtered read — only the broad `suite_id IN (...)` case is uncovered. Index choice there wants EXPLAIN evidence at real row counts, which is squarely the W6 scale-aware work. The issue carries the full table inventory and acceptance criteria, including that "measured: the planner ignores it at our volume" is a valid outcome.

**Finding 3 (drift) — fixed.** Each `count_*`/`list_*` pair now shares one filter chain (`_run_filters`, `_pipeline_run_filters`, `_incident_filters`). Frontend header parsing became one `toListPage` helper — placed in a **new `src/api/listPage.ts` rather than `client.ts`**, because every API test replaces `client.ts` wholesale with `vi.mock`; putting it there broke 7 tests and would have meant the mocks stubbed out the arithmetic. In its own module it stays at 100% coverage under those mocks.

## Second `/code-review` pass — 5 new findings, all fixed

The sharpest one was real and load-bearing: **`/runs` got the header but `listRuns` discarded it**, so the Results *Runs* tab — the primary runs surface and the whole reason for #1108 — still rendered its capped 200-row fetch as if complete. Fixed by returning a `RunListPage` and adding the same disclosure the Pipeline tab has (`RecentRuns` takes only `.items`; it's deliberately a "most recent 8" widget). Also fixed: the pipeline note counted the *unfiltered* page while the table rendered filtered rows (so "Showing the most recent 200 of 211" could sit above a 3-row table or the empty state), its advice to "narrow the provider or date filter" could never work since both selects are client-side over the already-fetched page, a stale comment calling `total` "filter-scoped", and two deprecated antd `Alert message` props. Both new tests mutation-checked.

The 422 being an **undeclared breaking change** was a fair call — I documented it explicitly in the PR body rather than leaving it implied.

## Notes

- The merge of `origin/main` (~75 files) was conflict-free — no manual resolution needed, `docs/progress.md` included.
- A repo hygiene test (`test_no_test_hides_a_request_inside_an_assert`) caught one of my own shortcuts — `assert client.get(...).status_code == 200` — which `python -O` would have deleted entirely. Fixed.
- Filed a follow-up docs PR [#1246](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1246) (merged) for the post-merge re-count: **28 in `v1.1 Backlog` / 45 repo-wide, unchanged** — #1108 closing and #1245 filing into the same milestone net out. Counts taken live from `gh issue list`, not predicted.
- Local branch `fix/issue-1108-paging-totals` still exists because the worktree at `.claude/worktrees/agent-aef7256da7da527b1` holds it; the remote branch was deleted. Remove the worktree when you want it gone.

A prior `/code-review` pass found several findings across multiple rounds. Use your judgment on fix-vs-file per CLAUDE.md's fixed-or-filed rule, but the FIRST one below is the most important and should be fixed, not filed:

1. **Access-control widening (fix this, it's a real new exposure):** `GET /orchestration/near-misses` is auth-only/workspace-wide unscoped — but `TriggerBinding` rows are suite-owned config that the sibling `GET /trigger-bindings` endpoint (`backend/app/api/v1/trigger_bindings.py`) already suite-scopes (`svc.list_bindings(db, user_id=current_user.id, ...)`, docstring "List trigger bindings on accessible suites"). This PR's new endpoint lets ANY authenticated user enumerate `(provider, pipeline_or_dag_id, binding_env)` for trigger bindings on suites they have zero access to — information `GET /trigger-bindings` would 403/omit for them. The route's docstring justifies this by analogy to `/orchestration/pipelines`, but that endpoint's data (`pipeline_runs`) is genuinely workspace-wide orchestrator telemetry with no suite-ownership concept, whereas `TriggerBinding` rows ARE suite-owned. Fix: scope the near-miss read to only bindings on suites the calling user can access, mirroring how `list_bindings` does it (likely via the same `accessible_suite_ids`-style filter used elsewhere in this codebase, e.g. in `run_service`/`incident_service`).

2. **Multiple-concurrent-near-misses-per-binding gap (fix if reasonably contained):** The frontend badge (`TriggerRow` in `TriggersPanel.tsx`) picks the FIRST matching near-miss via `.find()` when more than one could be simultaneously current for the same binding (e.g. two different orchestrator connections both reporting the same DAG id against different wrong envs — literally the #1186 root cause this whole feature exists to catch). This silently hides the second live mismatch. Also related: no `ORDER BY` on the `WorkspaceHealth` read query before the Python-side sort in `list_current_env_near_misses`, so result ordering isn't guaranteed on ties, compounding the above non-deterministically.

3. **Stale badge after disabling a binding:** disabling a binding (`onChanged` in `TriggersPanel.tsx`) only reloads the bindings list, never `nearMissState` — so a mismatch badge can persist on a binding the user just disabled, until the panel remounts. Fix if cheap (e.g. also trigger a near-miss refetch on `onChanged`).

Remote branch is gone (the earlier local ref was just stale). Everything is complete.

## Summary

**PR #1235 merged** (squash, `9a9dc957`), **#1199 closed**, branch deleted. Merged main first (clean, no conflicts).

### Findings addressed

**1. Access-control widening (fixed — this was the real one).** `GET /orchestration/near-misses` shipped auth-only by analogy to `/orchestration/pipelines`. The analogy was wrong: `pipeline_runs` is workspace-wide orchestrator telemetry with no suite-ownership concept, whereas a near-miss is derived *wholly* from `trigger_binding` rows — suite-owned config the sibling `GET /trigger-bindings` already scopes. As written, any signed-in user could enumerate `(provider, pipeline_or_dag_id, binding_env)` for bindings on suites they can't see. ---
name: project-issue-gt1000-triage-2026-08-08
description: "COMPLETE — all 16 fixable GitHub issues numbered >1000 fixed, reviewed, and merged; 8 follow-up issues filed and not yet picked up (list below)"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 23338a22-3fe4-41f8-b4f7-1c7ba861cfd6
  modified: 2026-08-09T09:22:16.430Z
---

**SWEEP COMPLETE as of 2026-08-09.** Spanning two sessions (2026-08-08 evening/night, resumed 2026-08-09), triaged all 19 open GitHub issues numbered >1000 on TheurgicDuke771/DataQ, excluded 3 (see below), and ran the remaining 16 through the full CLAUDE.md workflow (branch → implement → test → `/code-review` → PR → merge). `gh pr list --state open` confirmed zero open PRs from this sweep at completion.

**Two account monthly-spend-limit hits mid-flight** (agents killed by API error) — both recovered by the user raising the cap; all WIP was safely committed to worktrees each time, nothing was lost. **After the second interruption, execution switched from many-parallel-background-agents to one-agent-at-a-time** (user's explicit instruction) for the remaining ~7 issues — slower, but let each fix get full attention plus a genuine second `/code-review` pass before merging, which caught real bugs in nearly every one.

**Pattern worth remembering for future sweeps like this: nearly every PR that needed first-round review fixes had a SECOND round of real, previously-invisible bugs surface once the first-round fix landed** — e.g. #1108's header fix revealed the Results *Runs* tab was silently discarding the new header and still rendering a capped fetch as complete; #1193's credential-leak fix revealed a stale-preview relabeling bug; #1199's access-control fix revealed an outage-reads-as-healthy bug and a stale present-tense tooltip; #1104's robustness fixes revealed a second-order Snowflake privilege-filtering gap. **Always run `/code-review` again after fixing findings on an already-flagged PR — never assume one review pass is enough once a PR needed a fix.**

**Excluded from the sweep entirely (deliberate, not attempted):**
- **#1118** (SSRF via `*_secret_name`) — deliberately deferred to the RBAC epic (#740–#744) per the issue's own text.
- **#1030, #1032** (harness dbt GRANT hook / password-auth in deployed harness Terraform) — need a live Snowsight GRANT + Terraform apply against currently-stopped harness infra; not safe to do unattended.

## All 16 issues — final disposition

| Issue | PR(s) | Notable finding caught in review |
|---|---|---|
| #1195 | #1215 | — (trivial doc fix) |
| #1200 | #1217 | — (test hermeticity) |
| #1102 | #1216 | extended to `backend/alembic/env.py`; #1221 filed for pooled-connection gap |
| #1101 | #1225 | real bug: `dispatch.py` ignored `publish_health`'s bool return |
| #1205 | #1218 + #1232 | — |
| #1107 | #1224 | real bug: `AssetsTableView` never forwarded abort signal to `listAssets` |
| #1001 | #1222 + #1237 | real regression: `RangeReader` chunk size caused 6.8x MORE bytes than the whole-object download it replaced |
| #1196 | #1219 | part of the #1196→#1197→#1203 cluster |
| #1109 | #1220 | real regression: first-draft fix pruned cached lineage edges on every transient blip; second review round caught the fix's own inversion bug; #1228, #1236 filed |
| #1197 | #1238 | uncapped-comparison inversion caught by review; contract-drift in docstrings fixed |
| #1203 | #1240 | shared `sql.strip_statement_echo` applied at persist/dry-run/read choke points; same leak also found+fixed in `dryrun_service` |
| #1202 | #1223 | — (review was already clean; just needed a rebase) |
| #1104 | #1227 | unguarded commit could abort whole nightly sweep; missing row-lock (new shared `connection_lock.py`); stale ORM read after rollback; over-eager PERMISSION misclassification; #1242 filed |
| #1193 | #1233 | **credential/DSN leak** via raw `str(exc)` in HTTP error envelope; #1243 filed (unbounded/uncancellable listing + ReDoS) |
| #1108 | #1231 | #828-class gap: no status-vocabulary validation; second pass found Results *Runs* tab discarding the new header entirely; #1245 filed (index question) |
| #1199 | #1235 | **real access-control widening**: near-miss endpoint let any user enumerate suite-owned trigger-binding info; fixed with `accessible_suite_ids` scoping; #1247, #1248 filed |

## Follow-up issues filed this session — NOT YET PICKED UP
- **#1221** — pooled/idle DB connections have no timeout protection (only the initial connect does); `connect_timeout` doesn't cover a connection going silent mid-life.
- **#1228** — two remaining lineage abort-instead-of-descend sites (siblings of the #1109 fix).
- **#1236** — lineage prune-suspension (`prunable` flag) has no durable backstop; needs a migration to persist state across restarts.
- **#1242** — Snowflake's `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` is privilege-filtered not access-denied, so a role with zero grants enumerates zero rows and #1104 records that as a healthy sync — needs a new state + UI decision to distinguish from a genuinely empty database.
- **#1243** — `/suites/{id}/batch-preview` (#1193) does an unbounded, uncancellable, blocking object listing on every keystroke pause with no `AbortController`, and now runs a user-supplied regex on the API process for the first time (ReDoS surface, `re` holds the GIL). Needs a design change (streaming/paging/timeout), not a line fix.
- **#1245** — no composite index backs the new `(created_at, id)` paging tie-break on `runs`/`pipeline_runs`/`incidents`; needs EXPLAIN evidence at real row counts before sizing (W6 scale-aware-execution scope).
- **#1247** — the near-miss read side (`list_current_env_near_misses`) hash-guesses candidate tuples rather than reading stored decodable data; coupled to the write side only by a prose comment, not shared code.
- **#1248** — **pre-existing, unrelated to this sweep**: 4 of #1193's batch-preview tests fail under `SECRET_STORE=openbao` (the local-stack default since #1159). Reproduced on a clean `origin/main` checkout — will cost every future contributor a false-alarm triage round until fixed.

None of these 8 are picked up yet. Worth a future session or explicit ask before starting any of them — several (#1236, #1243) need a real design decision, not just an implementation.

Audits whether the covering tests hand-build the value in the shape our model expects (the "fixture encodes our model" defect that hid (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- entire-search: Search Entire checkpoint history and transcripts with `entire search --json`. Use proactively when the user asks about previous work, commits, sessions, prompts, or historical context in this repository. (Tools: Bash)

"API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. - orchestration-abstraction-guard: Specialized reviewer that audits backend code for provider-specific branching that bypasses the OrchestrationProvider abstraction. Use this proactively when reviewing any PR that touches backend/app/orchestration/, backend/app/services/, or backend/app/api/ — especially any code path handling ADF or Airflow events, trigger bindings, or pipeline_runs. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). {"body":"Follow-up from the #1102 code review (found by the code-review agent on PR #1216).

## What

PR #1216 added `connect_args={"connect_timeout": 10}` to the shared engine in `backend/app/db/session.py`, closing the gap where an unreachable DB blocked every `get_session()` caller on the OS/driver's *initial connect* default.

`connect_timeout` only bounds establishing a **brand-new** libpq/psycopg2 connection. It does nothing for a connection that was already open and pooled when a network partition happens *later*.

## Failure scenario

The API has been running for a while with warm pooled connections. A network partition occurs (route drops silently, no TCP RST) after those connections were already established. A caller does `get_session()` → `SessionLocal()` checks out an already-connected pooled connection; `pool_pre_ping=True` issues a `SELECT 1` on that existing socket. Neither `connect_timeout` (initial connect only) nor `lock_timeout` (a lock-wait GUC, not a general statement/read timeout) bounds this read — it can hang indefinitely, including inside the #1052 staleness loop's graceful-shutdown await (`staleness_stop.set(); await staleness_task`) that #1102 was trying to protect.

## Why this is a separate issue, not folded into #1102/#1216

Closing this needs a different mechanism than `connect_timeout` — most likely TCP keepalives (`keepalives`, `keepalives_idle`, `keepalives_interval`, `keepalives_count` psycopg2 `connect_args`) so a dead socket is detected and reaped instead of hanging on a read with no data ever arriving. `statement_timeout` was deliberately rejected in `session.py`'s existing comments (a long-running GX query is legitimate). Keepalive tuning needs its own design/testing pass (values, whether it's safe across all supported Postgres providers e.g. Azure PostgreSQL Flexible Server, and verification that it actually kicks in for a black-holed connection) rather than a one-line addition alongside #1102's narrower fix.

## Suggested direction

Add TCP keepalive `connect_args` (e.g. `keepalives=1, keepalives_idle=30, keepalives_interval=10, keepalives_count=3`) to the same engine in `backend/app/db/session.py`, verified against a simulated black-holed connection (e.g. via a firewall rule dropping packets silently, not just closing the socket) rather than unit-tested only, since this crosses the same "only a live/real-network test is evidence" class as the driver-boundary lesson already recorded in CLAUDE.md.

{"body":"Found by the `/code-review` passes on #1220 (the #1109 fix) and deliberately deferred there to keep that PR's scope on the prune regression. **Two sites, same shape, one PR fixes both.**

Both are the #1109 shape at a different point in the ladder: work that already succeeded is thrown away because a *later* read failed, when descending would have persisted a real graph.

## Site 1 — an unclassified ACCESS_HISTORY failure aborts the pull

`SnowflakeLineageProvider.fetch_edges` reads the OBJECT_DEPENDENCIES floor **first**, successfully, and only then calls `_from_access_history`. That call classifies its failure through `_reraise_if_feature_unsupported` — an edition gate or a grant denial is skipped with an honest reason — but **anything else re-raises** and propagates straight out of `fetch_edges`:

```python
        except Exception as exc:
            _reraise_if_feature_unsupported(exc)
            raise
```

So a transient blip on the ACCESS_HISTORY query throws away the floor's already-successful current-state read and costs the whole refresh.

## Site 2 — a floor failure AFTER a successful GET_LINEAGE traversal aborts the pull

In the top-tier path, `top.edges` is a *successful, rich* GET_LINEAGE traversal. If the subsequent `_from_object_dependencies` read then fails, everything — including that traversal — is discarded and `WarehouseLineageUnavailableError` is raised, so the refresh returns `None` and writes nothing.

Note this one is a genuine judgement call, not an obvious bug: the floor is the current-state authority, so a result without it is arguably not prunable at all. That is precisely what `prunable=False` now expresses, which is what makes descending here safe where it previously was not.

## Why both are lower severity than #1109 (and still worth fixing)

They are **safe**, not merely less bad: `refresh_warehouse_edges` catches the escaping exception fail-soft, returns `None`, and the cache is left untouched (no prune, no data loss). The cost is a **lost refresh cycle** plus a `lineage_last_error` on the connection — where a descent would have persisted a real graph and said `access_history: call failed (<ExcType>) (transient — retried next refresh)`.

The machinery to do this correctly now exists after #1220: `_FeatureUnsupportedError(..., transient=True)` + `WarehouseLineageResult.prunable=False` means either descent can be made without re-introducing the prune regression #1220 fixed. `fetch_edges`'s `partial` flag already ORs in `exc.transient` from the ACCESS_HISTORY handler.

## AC

- [ ] An unclassified `_from_access_history` failure skips just that tier, with a classified reason (exception TYPE only — the #902 rule), and the floor's edges are returned
- [ ] A floor failure after a SUCCESSFUL GET_LINEAGE traversal returns the traversal's edges rather than discarding them — or the decision to keep raising is recorded with its reasoning
- [ ] Both descents carry `prunable=False` (transient skip → the refresh accretes, never prunes — #1220), and `degraded_reason` names the transient skip

{"body":"Found by the `/code-review` pass on #1220 and deliberately deferred there (it needs a persisted marker, i.e. a migration, which #1220 explicitly has none of).

## What

#1220 introduced `WarehouseLineageResult.prunable`: a snapshot pull that only PARTIALLY observed current state (a tier skipped or half-traversed for a transient reason) is persisted accrete-only, with no stale-edge prune. Its module docstring promises:

> The next clean pull prunes normally, so a genuinely removed dependency is at worst one cycle late — the cheap side of the trade.

**Nothing enforces that a clean pull ever arrives.** Any *persistent* condition that reads as transient — a statement timeout on call 1 every cycle, a driver-shape error that `_feature_unsupported_reason`'s two narrow patterns don't match — leaves `authoritative_snapshot` False on every refresh, and `lineage_edges` accretes indefinitely with no prune. The promise degrades from "one cycle late" to "never", silently.

(The likeliest concrete path — a confirmed per-object denial recurring every cycle — was closed inside #1220 itself: only UNCLASSIFIED failures set `prunable=False`. What is left is the genuinely-unclassifiable-but-persistent case.)

## Current mitigation, and why it is not enough

#1220 emits `warehouse_lineage_prune_suspended` at WARNING on every suspended cycle, so the condition is alertable in App Insights, and `lineage_degraded_reason` carries the transient tag on the connection. But:

- `WarehouseRefreshOutcome` does not carry the suspension, so no API/UI surface can report it.
- Nothing records **how long** it has been suspended — an operator cannot distinguish "blipped once last night" from "has not pruned in three weeks", which is precisely the #828/#1091 class of blindness (a real problem the product reports as merely 'degraded').

## Options (pick at design time)

1. **Bounded suspension.** Persist `lineage_last_authoritative_refresh_at`; once it is older than `LINEAGE_STALE_AFTER_HOURS` (already defined, default 48h), prune anyway on the next successful pull — a stale-but-honest graph beats an unboundedly accreting one. Needs one nullable timestamp column.
2. **Report it.** Plumb the suspension (and its age) through `WarehouseRefreshOutcome` → connection state → `warehouse_lineage_status`, so the existing lineage banner says "pruning suspended since X".

(1) and (2) are complementary; (2) alone is the honest-degradation minimum, (1) is the self-healing one.

## AC

- [ ] A snapshot connection whose prune has been suspended for longer than the configured threshold is either pruned anyway or visibly reported as suspended (with an age) on a product surface, not only in logs
- [ ] The choice is recorded in `warehouse_refresh`'s module docstring, which currently states the unenforced "at worst one cycle late" promise
- [ ] Test covering N consecutive partial cycles, asserting the backstop fires","labels":[{"id":"LA_kwDOSBITx88AAAACfH8OBQ","name":"enhancement","description":"New feature or request","color":"a2eeef"}],"milestone":{"number":4,"title":"v1.1 Backlog","description":"Un-scheduled post-v1 backlog for the v1.1 cycle (renamed 2026-07-04 from 'Backlog (post-v1 / testing)'). New post-v1 issues land here by default.","dueOn":null},"number":1236,"state":"OPEN","title":"lineage: a suspended snapshot prune has no durable, product-visible backstop — it can stay suspended indefinitely"}

{"body":"## What

`inventory_service.sync_connection_inventory` returns `0` and the sweep records the tick as **healthy** (`inventory_sync_last_error = NULL`) when the enumeration query runs fine but returns **no rows**.

That is correct for a genuinely empty database — and wrong for the case #1104 was filed about. Snowflake's `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` is **privilege-filtered, not access-denied**: a role with no grants on the objects gets an empty result set, not an error. So the Snowflake half of the #1104 scenario still lands exactly where the issue started:

- toggle on
- connection test green (`SELECT 1` never exercises the enumeration query)
- zero assets ever appear
- **no badge, no error, nothing says why** — the sync reports success

Unity Catalog raises on a missing `SELECT` on `system.information_schema`, so #1104's classifier covers that half; the Snowflake half is this issue.

## Why it isn't just "record an error"

A brand-new / deliberately empty database legitimately enumerates zero tables, and calling that a failure would be a false alarm on the connections list — the same confident-wrong-answer failure mode in the other direction. So this needs a distinct, honest state rather than reusing `inventory_sync_last_error`, e.g.:

- a synced-table count (or "synced, 0 tables visible") state surfaced as a neutral informational note, not an error badge; and/or
- a transition signal — a connection that used to enumerate N>0 and now enumerates 0 IS worth flagging, since privilege loss and a dropped database both look like that.

Deciding which is the work; the code change is small either way.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An opted-in connection whose enumeration returns zero tables is distinguishable in the product from one that has never synced and from one that synced N>0.
- [ ] An empty-by-design database does **not** render as an error/failure.
- [ ] A drop from N>0 to 0 is surfaced (this is the privilege-loss signal).
- [ ] Test covering: zero-row enumeration, and the N>0 → 0 transition.

Both are the #1109 shape at a different point in the ladder: work that already succeeded is thrown away because a *later* read failed, when descending would have persisted a real graph.

## Site 1 — an unclassified ACCESS_HISTORY failure aborts the pull

`SnowflakeLineageProvider.fetch_edges` reads the OBJECT_DEPENDENCIES floor **first**, successfully, and only then calls `_from_access_history`. That call classifies its failure through `_reraise_if_feature_unsupported` — an edition gate or a grant denial is skipped with an honest reason — but **anything else re-raises** and propagates straight out of `fetch_edges`:

```python
        except Exception as exc:
            _reraise_if_feature_unsupported(exc)
            raise
```

So a transient blip on the ACCESS_HISTORY query throws away the floor's already-successful current-state read and costs the whole refresh.

## Site 2 — a floor failure AFTER a successful GET_LINEAGE traversal aborts the pull

In the top-tier path, `top.edges` is a *successful, rich* GET_LINEAGE traversal. If the subsequent `_from_object_dependencies` read then fails, everything — including that traversal — is discarded and `WarehouseLineageUnavailableError` is raised, so the refresh returns `None` and writes nothing.

Note this one is a genuine judgement call, not an obvious bug: the floor is the current-state authority, so a result without it is arguably not prunable at all. That is precisely what `prunable=False` now expresses, which is what makes descending here safe where it previously was not.

## Why both are lower severity than #1109 (and still worth fixing)

They are **safe**, not merely less bad: `refresh_warehouse_edges` catches the escaping exception fail-soft, returns `None`, and the cache is left untouched (no prune, no data loss). The cost is a **lost refresh cycle** plus a `lineage_last_error` on the connection — where a descent would have persisted a real graph and said `access_history: call failed (<ExcType>) (transient — retried next refresh)`.

The machinery to do this correctly now exists after #1220: `_FeatureUnsupportedError(..., transient=True)` + `WarehouseLineageResult.prunable=False` means either descent can be made without re-introducing the prune regression #1220 fixed. `fetch_edges`'s `partial` flag already ORs in `exc.transient` from the ACCESS_HISTORY handler.

- [ ] A floor failure after a SUCCESSFUL GET_LINEAGE traversal returns the traversal's edges rather than discarding them — or the decision to keep raising is recorded with its reasoning

{"body":"Found by the `/code-review` pass on #1220 and deliberately deferred there (it needs a persisted marker, i.e. a migration, which #1220 explicitly has none of).

## What

#1220 introduced `WarehouseLineageResult.prunable`: a snapshot pull that only PARTIALLY observed current state (a tier skipped or half-traversed for a transient reason) is persisted accrete-only, with no stale-edge prune. Its module docstring promises:

> The next clean pull prunes normally, so a genuinely removed dependency is at worst one cycle late — the cheap side of the trade.

**Nothing enforces that a clean pull ever arrives.** Any *persistent* condition that reads as transient — a statement timeout on call 1 every cycle, a driver-shape error that `_feature_unsupported_reason`'s two narrow patterns don't match — leaves `authoritative_snapshot` False on every refresh, and `lineage_edges` accretes indefinitely with no prune. The promise degrades from "one cycle late" to "never", silently.

(The likeliest concrete path — a confirmed per-object denial recurring every cycle — was closed inside #1220 itself: only UNCLASSIFIED failures set `prunable=False`. What is left is the genuinely-unclassifiable-but-persistent case.)

## Current mitigation, and why it is not enough

#1220 emits `warehouse_lineage_prune_suspended` at WARNING on every suspended cycle, so the condition is alertable in App Insights, and `lineage_degraded_reason` carries the transient tag on the connection. But:

- `WarehouseRefreshOutcome` does not carry the suspension, so no API/UI surface can report it.
- Nothing records **how long** it has been suspended — an operator cannot distinguish "blipped once last night" from "has not pruned in three weeks", which is precisely the #828/#1091 class of blindness (a real problem the product reports as merely 'degraded').

## Options (pick at design time)

1. **Bounded suspension.** Persist `lineage_last_authoritative_refresh_at`; once it is older than `LINEAGE_STALE_AFTER_HOURS` (already defined, default 48h), prune anyway on the next successful pull — a stale-but-honest graph beats an unboundedly accreting one. Needs one nullable timestamp column.
2. **Report it.** Plumb the suspension (and its age) through `WarehouseRefreshOutcome` → connection state → `warehouse_lineage_status`, so the existing lineage banner says "pruning suspended since X".

(1) and (2) are complementary; (2) alone is the honest-degradation minimum, (1) is the self-healing one.

## AC

- [ ] A snapshot connection whose prune has been suspended for longer than the configured threshold is either pruned anyway or visibly reported as suspended (with an age) on a product surface, not only in logs

{"body":"## What

`inventory_service.sync_connection_inventory` returns `0` and the sweep records the tick as **healthy** (`inventory_sync_last_error = NULL`) when the enumeration query runs fine but returns **no rows**.

That is correct for a genuinely empty database — and wrong for the case #1104 was filed about. Snowflake's `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` is **privilege-filtered, not access-denied**: a role with no grants on the objects gets an empty result set, not an error. So the Snowflake half of the #1104 scenario still lands exactly where the issue started:

- toggle on
- connection test green (`SELECT 1` never exercises the enumeration query)
- zero assets ever appear
- **no badge, no error, nothing says why** — the sync reports success

Unity Catalog raises on a missing `SELECT` on `system.information_schema`, so #1104's classifier covers that half; the Snowflake half is this issue.

## Why it isn't just "record an error"

A brand-new / deliberately empty database legitimately enumerates zero tables, and calling that a failure would be a false alarm on the connections list — the same confident-wrong-answer failure mode in the other direction. So this needs a distinct, honest state rather than reusing `inventory_sync_last_error`, e.g.:

- a synced-table count (or "synced, 0 tables visible") state surfaced as a neutral informational note, not an error badge; and/or
- a transition signal — a connection that used to enumerate N>0 and now enumerates 0 IS worth flagging, since privilege loss and a dropped database both look like that.

{"body":"Filed from the `/code-review` pass on PR #1233 (batch-target preview, #1193). Deferred out of that PR because the fix is a design change (bounds + cancellation), not a line edit, and the endpoint is authenticated + edit-gated + rate-limited, so this is a hardening gap rather than an open door.

## What

`GET /api/v1/suites/{id}/batch-preview` (`preview_batch_target` in `backend/app/api/v1/suites.py`, service `run_target.preview_batch`) is a **sync** endpoint that does a **live object listing** under the caller's prefix and matches a **caller-supplied regex** against every key. Two consequences:

1. **Thread-pool pressure.** Sync endpoints run in Starlette's bounded threadpool (40 threads by default). The listing is bounded only by `flatfile._BATCH_LISTING_MAX` (500,000 objects) with no wall-clock timeout and no cancellation. The frontend `BatchPreviewHint` auto-fires it on form mount and on every 400 ms typing pause, and it does not `AbortController`-cancel a superseded request (it only ignores the result). One author on a broad prefix can therefore hold several threads for a long time and stall every other sync endpoint in the API.

   This differs from the run path, where the same listing happens **in the Celery worker**, and from the dry-run/profiler endpoints, which are bounded by the datasource's own query timeout rather than by an object count.

2. **ReDoS surface moved into the API.** `run_target.resolve_target` already `re.compile`s a user pattern in the API process at save time, but *matching* it against arbitrary keys previously only ever happened in the worker. This endpoint is the first place the API process runs a user regex over attacker-influenceable input (object key names), so a catastrophic-backtracking pattern now pins an API thread instead of a worker.

## Suggested direction

- A wall-clock/object budget for the *preview* specifically, well below `_BATCH_LISTING_MAX` — a preview does not need to be exhaustive to be useful, and "scanned the first N and found no match" is an honest answer we can render (the honesty bar #1105 set for asset truncation).
- Client-side `AbortController` on supersession in `BatchPreviewHint`, so a fast typist doesn't leave N in-flight listings behind.
- Consider moving the preview off the sync path (or onto the worker) if the budget can't be made tight enough.
- Bound the regex work — a length cap on the pattern, and/or a per-key match budget.

## Acceptance

- A preview against a very large prefix returns within a bounded time with an honest partial answer, and cannot hold an API thread indefinitely.
- Superseded preview requests are cancelled client-side, not merely ignored.
- A pathological backtracking pattern cannot pin an API worker thread.","labels":[{"id":"LA_kwDOSBITx88AAAACfH8N5g","name":"bug","description":"Something isn't working","color":"d73a4a"}],"milestone":{"number":4,"title":"v1.1 Backlog","description":"Un-scheduled post-v1 backlog for the v1.1 cycle (renamed 2026-07-04 from 'Backlog (post-v1 / testing)'). {"body":"## Context

#1108 (PR #1231) gave `/runs`, `/pipeline_runs` and `/incidents` an `X-Total-Count` header and, for `/runs`, `offset` paging plus a total-order `(created_at DESC, id DESC)` tie-break. All three list endpoints now page the same way:

| endpoint | table | order | max `limit` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GET /runs` | `runs` | `created_at DESC, id DESC` | 200 |
| `GET /pipeline_runs` | `pipeline_runs` | `created_at DESC, id DESC` | 200 |
| `GET /incidents` | `incidents` | `created_at DESC, id DESC` | 500 |

**None of the three tables has an index that matches that ordering.** Today they carry only single-column indexes:

- `runs` — `ix_runs_suite_id`, `ix_runs_status`, `ix_runs_asset_id`, plus the composite `ix_runs_suite_created` on `(suite_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)`
- `pipeline_runs` — `ix_pipeline_runs_provider_pipeline`, `ix_pipeline_runs_connection_id`
- `incidents` — `ix_incidents_asset_id`, `ix_incidents_check_id`, `ix_incidents_suite_id`, `ix_incidents_status`

`ix_runs_suite_created` covers the *suite-scoped* read (`?suite_id=`) and the `datasource_health` LATERAL from #999. It does **not** cover the unfiltered list, which is `suite_id IN (<every accessible suite>)` — the default Results-page read and the whole workspace-admin view. That plan is a full scan + sort, and `OFFSET` makes it worse linearly: the database materialises and discards every skipped row on every page.

## Why this is filed rather than fixed in #1231

- The gap is **identical on all three tables**, and is pre-existing on two of them (`pipeline_runs` since #928, `incidents` since #772). Adding an ad-hoc index to `runs` alone inside a header-shaped PR would be an arbitrary partial fix.
- Index choice here wants **EXPLAIN evidence at real row counts**, not a guess. Prod's `runs`/`incidents` tables are currently small enough that the planner may prefer a seq scan regardless, so an index added now could be dead weight that only costs write amplification.
- This is purely a performance concern — **no correctness or honesty defect**. The totals and the paging are correct today; they are just not cheap at depth.

It belongs with the "v1.1 W6 scale-aware execution" work, which is where the row-count growth assumptions get made.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Capture `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` for each of the three list queries at a realistic row count (seeded, or prod if the volume is there) — both the unfiltered read and the common filtered ones (`?suite_id=`, `?status=`, `?provider=`, `?state=`).
- [ ] Decide per table whether a `(created_at DESC, id DESC)` composite (or a filter-leading variant such as `(status, created_at DESC, id DESC)`) actually changes the plan. **Record the evidence, including a decision not to add one** — a measured "the planner ignores it at our volume" is a valid and useful outcome.
- [ ] If added: an additive index-only migration (no data change, no column change), tested up **and** down locally, with the model `__table_args__` kept in sync.
- [ ] Consider whether `OFFSET` should give way to keyset/seek paging on the deepest surface — the ordering is already total, which is the precondition for it.

## Not in scope

Changing the response contract. `X-Total-Count` and the current `limit`/`offset` parameters stay as #1108 shipped them.

{"body":"Follow-up filed from the `/code-review` pass on #1235 (fixes #1199). Not a correctness bug today — filed rather than dropped, per CONTRIBUTING rule 3a.

## What

`workspace_health.key` is an opaque SHA-256 hash by design: the identifying tuple `(provider, pipeline_or_dag_id, run_env, binding_env)` can run to ~256 chars (Airflow DAG ids) against a 64-char PK column, so there is nothing to `SELECT` a tuple back out of.

The #1199 read path (`workspace_health_service.list_current_env_near_misses`) therefore works by **re-deriving candidate tuples and hash-probing**: it enumerates every ENABLED `trigger_binding`'s `(provider, pipeline_or_dag_id, env)`, crosses it with the other three members of the closed `ENVS` vocabulary as candidate `run_env`s, hashes each with the same `_near_miss_key` the write side uses, and keeps the hashes that exist as real rows.

That means the read side's candidate-selection logic must stay in lock-step with the **write** side's (`orchestration_service._record_env_near_misses`) — and today the only thing coupling them is a prose comment in each. The shared code is just `_near_miss_key`; the *choice of which tuples get hashed* is duplicated.

#1235 added `TestNearMissWriteReadRoundTrip` (a test that drives the real production write path and asserts the read side decodes it, plus a disabled-binding case), which turns a future desync into a red test rather than a silent one. This issue is about removing the duplication itself.

## Options (pick at design time)

1. **Store the tuple.** Add a nullable JSONB `detail` column (or a sibling `near_miss` table) alongside the hashed key, so the read is a plain `SELECT` and no candidate derivation exists at all. Costs a migration; ends the coupling outright. Probably the right answer.
2. **Extract one shared derivation.** A single function both sides call, e.g. `candidate_near_miss_tuples(...)`, so there is exactly one definition of "which tuples are eligible."
3. Leave as-is and rely on the round-trip test.

## Also in scope (cheap, related)

`TriggersPanel` fetches near-misses on every mount with no caching. #1235 narrowed it to `?suite_id=` so it no longer pulls the whole accessible workspace on each suite switch, but it still fires for suites with zero trigger bindings (the alternative — gating the fetch on the bindings result — would serialise the two requests into a waterfall, which is worse). A shared cache across suite switches would remove the redundant call entirely.

## Acceptance

- Only one place in the codebase decides which `(provider, pipeline_or_dag_id, run_env, binding_env)` tuples constitute a near-miss.
- The #1235 round-trip tests still pass unchanged (they assert behaviour, not structure).

{"body":"Found while running the local backend gate for #1235. **Pre-existing on `origin/main`** (reproduced there in a clean detached worktree at `5db041c7`), so it is not a regression from that PR — filed rather than dropped, per CONTRIBUTING rule 3a.

## Symptom

Four of the batch-target preview tests added by #1233 fail locally whenever the developer's `.env.app` configures a real secret store:

```
FAILED backend/tests/api/test_suites.py::test_batch_preview_returns_resolved_path
FAILED backend/tests/api/test_suites.py::test_batch_preview_no_match_returns_422
FAILED backend/tests/api/test_suites.py::test_batch_preview_listing_too_large_returns_422
FAILED backend/tests/api/test_suites.py::test_batch_preview_default_strategy_is_latest
```

with

```
assert resp.status_code == 200
E   assert 502 == 200

[info   ] secret_store_initialized  backend=openbao
[warning] batch_preview_failed      connection_type=s3 error_type=SecretNotFoundError
[warning] dataq_error               code=batch_preview_failed status=502
```

They pass with `SECRET_STORE=env` and fail with `SECRET_STORE=openbao`. Since ADR 0039 / #1159 the local stack's `.env.app` ships `SECRET_STORE=openbao`, so this is now the *default* local experience.

## Cause

`_s3_suite` builds its connection via `_typed_connection(...)`, which inserts the `Connection` ORM row directly with a placeholder `secret_ref` — no secret is ever written to the configured store. The tests then stub the *listing* (`_patch_resolve_batch_file`) but not the **secret read** that `batch-preview` performs before it, so with a real store attached the endpoint legitimately 502s on `SecretNotFoundError`.

Sibling tests in the same file avoid this by stubbing further out (`_patch_dataframe`), which is why only the batch-preview four fail.

## Why it matters beyond the annoyance

A test whose result depends on ambient developer environment is a test that can be green for the wrong reason, and this class has bitten the project before. It also costs every contributor a false-alarm triage round before they can trust their own gate — I lost one to it.

## Fix (suggested)

Stub the secret resolution in the batch-preview tests the way the listing is already stubbed (or have `_s3_suite` provision a secret into whichever store is configured), so the four tests assert the preview logic regardless of `SECRET_STORE`.

## Acceptance

- `pytest backend/tests/api/test_suites.py -k batch_preview` passes with `SECRET_STORE` set to `env` **and** to `openbao`.
